lead: Ultrasound is sound above 20 kHz, beyond hearing. A thin quartz plate, silvered on both faces and held between metal plates, is driven by a radio-frequency oscillator. The crystal changes thickness when a voltage is applied — the inverse piezoelectric effect — and at its thickness resonance it vibrates strongly and radiates an ultrasonic beam. The frequency comes from the plate's own thickness, not from the circuit, so it stays stable. Such transducers drive cleaning tanks, weld testing, medical scanners and sonar.
prereq: You need: 2.1 Simple harmonic motion and 2.3 resonance; the plated crystal is a driven oscillator.

blocks.text: Squeeze certain crystals and charge appears on their faces, proportional to the stress and vanishing when it is removed. This is the piezoelectric effect. Quartz, Rochelle salt, barium titanate and lead zirconate titanate (PZT) show it. PZT is a cheap, strong ceramic; quartz is precise and stable.

The reverse also holds. Apply a voltage across those faces and the plate changes thickness; reverse the voltage and it shrinks instead of swelling. This is the inverse piezoelectric effect. An alternating voltage therefore makes the plate expand and contract at the supply frequency, pushing the surrounding air or water and starting a pressure wave. Production of ultrasound uses the inverse effect; detection uses the direct effect.
Construction: a crystal slab ground flat and parallel, silvered on both faces to form electrodes, and clamped between two metal plates that hold it and connect it to the circuit.

The plated plate is a vibrator with its own natural frequency, like a tuning fork. Its faces are free, so they swing with maximum amplitude while the middle stays still. That fundamental standing-wave pattern (2.5) fits half a wavelength into the thickness: λ = 2t.

blocks.where: f is the fundamental thickness-resonance frequency in hertz; v is the longitudinal speed of sound in the crystal in m/s (about 5.7 × 10³ m/s for quartz); t is the plate thickness in metres.

blocks.text: Drive the plate at that frequency and its amplitude grows sharply — resonance, as with a pushed swing (2.3). Drive it elsewhere and it barely moves. Since t is fixed by grinding and v belongs to the crystal, f is fixed too. Thin plates give high frequencies: 2 mm of quartz gives about 1.4 MHz, 0.2 mm gives about 14 MHz. Harmonics 3f and 5f exist but are weaker; above about 20 MHz quartz becomes too fragile and PZT is used.

A radio-frequency oscillator feeds the two electrodes. Usually the crystal itself sits in the oscillator's feedback path, so the circuit locks to the crystal resonance and cannot drift. Only a few universities teach the circuit details; the principle is what the exam asks.

items: High frequency: megahertz from a plate a millimetre thick.
Stable: frequency is set by thickness, not by a coil or capacitor.
Rugged, small, cheap and low power.
One plate both transmits and, from a returning echo, generates a voltage by the direct effect.

blocks.text: Ultrasound means f > 20 kHz. Cleaning and flaw detection use 1–10 MHz; at 1 MHz in water (v = 1500 m/s) the wavelength is 1.5 mm. Applications are in 2.8.

figure.caption: An oscillator applies an alternating voltage to the plated faces of the quartz plate; the plate strains at the same rate and, at resonance, sends out an ultrasonic beam.

examples.question: A quartz plate 2.0 mm thick is used to produce ultrasound. The longitudinal speed of sound in quartz along the cut is 5.7 × 10³ m/s. (a) Find the fundamental thickness-resonance frequency. (b) Find the wavelength inside the crystal. (c) Find the frequency if the plate is lapped down to 1.0 mm.
steps: Convert the thickness: t = 2.0 mm = 2.0 × 10⁻³ m.
At the fundamental, half a wavelength fits the thickness: λ = 2t = 2 × 2.0 × 10⁻³ = 4.0 × 10⁻³ m.
(c) With t = 1.0 × 10⁻³ m, f = 5700 ÷ (2 × 1.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.85 × 10⁶ Hz = 2.85 MHz; halving the thickness doubles the frequency.
examples.answer: The 2.0 mm plate resonates at 1.425 × 10⁶ Hz (1.43 MHz) with a wavelength of 4.0 × 10⁻³ m inside the crystal; at 1.0 mm the frequency is 2.85 × 10⁶ Hz.
examples.check:
v = 5.7e3
t = 2.0e-3
f = v / (2 * t)
lam = 2 * t
f2 = v / (2 * 1.0e-3)
print(f)
print(lam)
print(f2)

traps: Using the full thickness as one wavelength: the faces are antinodes, so t = λ/2 and f = v/(2t). The wrong answer v/t is twice the correct frequency.
Confusing the two effects: production is the inverse piezoelectric effect (voltage gives strain); the direct effect (strain gives voltage) is the receiver.
Putting the wrong speed in v: use the longitudinal speed in the crystal (about 5.7 × 10³ m/s for quartz), not 343 m/s for air or 1500 m/s for water.
Forgetting to convert millimetres to metres, which gives a frequency 1000 times too small.
Defining ultrasound as loud sound. It is sound above 20 kHz; loudness is a separate matter of amplitude.

quiz.q: Define the piezoelectric effect and the inverse piezoelectric effect.
quiz.a: Direct effect: mechanical stress on certain crystals produces charge on their faces, proportional to the stress and vanishing with it. Inverse effect: an applied voltage across the faces produces strain, a change of thickness.

quiz.q: Why is the frequency of a piezoelectric transducer set by the crystal rather than by the oscillator circuit?
quiz.a: The plate responds strongly only near its thickness resonance f = v/(2t). Placed in the feedback path, it forces the oscillator to run at that frequency, which depends on thickness and on the crystal's sound speed, not on any coil or capacitor.

quiz.q: At the fundamental resonance, why is the middle of the plate a node?
quiz.a: The two faces are free and vibrate with maximum amplitude, so they are antinodes. Half a wavelength fits across the thickness, and the midpoint of a half-wave pattern is a displacement node.

quiz.q: A PZT plate 0.50 mm thick has v = 4.0 × 10³ m/s. Find its fundamental thickness-resonance frequency.
A quartz plate must resonate at 5.0 MHz; v = 5.7 × 10³ m/s. Find the required thickness.
A single quartz plate transmits a pulse and then receives its echo. Which piezoelectric effect acts in each case, and what does the circuit measure?
quiz.a: Transmission uses the inverse effect: the oscillator voltage strains the plate and launches the pulse. Reception uses the direct effect: the returning pressure strains the plate and puts charge on the electrodes. The circuit measures that small voltage; the time delay gives distance.

quiz.q: A design needs 10 MHz. Quartz and PZT have similar sound speeds. Give one reason to prefer PZT and one drawback of very thin plates.
quiz.a: Both need t = v/(2f), roughly 0.3 mm. PZT has stronger electromechanical coupling, so it gives a larger output for the same drive, and it is cheaper and not fragile. Drawback: plates of a few tenths of a millimetre are hard to grind and easy to break, and thin quartz is the worst case.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern probes use PZT ceramics, and research uses single crystals such as PMN-PT for stronger coupling, plus capacitive micromachined ultrasonic transducers (CMUTs) and piezoelectric micromachined transducers (PMUTs) built by silicon micromachining. Thin films of aluminium nitride or zinc oxide can be sputtered straight onto a silicon chip, giving arrays of tiny transmitters for medical imaging. The key material number is the thickness coupling coefficient, which sets how much electrical drive turns into sound. Search for PMUT, CMUT and thickness-mode coupling coefficient if you want to go further.
